title: Sky Fortress
description: Build a floating fortress with a drawbridge, defense towers, and a secret laboratory.
steps: Sketch your fortress from above using squares and triangles.
Build three prototypes in Pocket Builder with different foundations.
Rebuild your favorite in a Luanti creative world; test the drawbridge mechanism.
Give your brother a guided tour and explain what holds the structure together.
hints: Begin with a 5×5 platform and add two supporting columns. A simple model beats a perfect plan.
brothers: One brother builds defenses; the other designs secret doors, then swap.
stretch: Calculate how many blocks a 20×20 platform needs and compare three material choices.

title: Robot Rescue Squad
description: Invent a robot that detects something and responds with light, sound, or movement.
steps: Draw a diagram of input → logic → output.
Test an LED and sensor in simulation before wiring.
With an adult, wire a low-voltage Pico 2 W circuit and write a short MicroPython program.
Measure false alarms and improve your design.
hints: Start with a blinking LED. Then choose a sensor that makes the light react to something real.
brothers: One codes the reaction; the other builds the protective case, then swap.
stretch: Add a second sensor and make the program respond to combinations.

title: Terraform Mars (Carefully!)
description: Build a Mars base where every design choice has to survive actual engineering constraints.
steps: Research Martian temperature, pressure, water, radiation, and energy needs.
Design a habitat plan with areas for air, water, food, and power.
Build a base in Luanti and annotate each life-support system.
Write down what is physically feasible and what is still science fiction.
hints: Begin with one question: where would the first settlers get breathable oxygen?
brothers: One investigates energy and water; the other designs habitats and food systems.
stretch: Calculate daily energy and water requirements for four imaginary astronauts.

title: Pixel Pal: The Game
description: Design a friendly creature, animate it, then program a playable adventure.
steps: Draw an 8-frame animation with a consistent silhouette.
Create simple obstacles and rewards in Scratch.
Use variables to control the creature’s energy and speed.
Invite your brother to playtest and change two things from his feedback.
hints: First make the character move left and right. Your art can improve after the game works.
brothers: One makes art and levels; the other codes the game, then switch.
stretch: Give the creature a behavior that reacts to the player’s actions.

title: The Bridge That Shouldn’t Stand
description: Try to cross an impossible canyon using geometry, forces, and clever design.
steps: Build three paper-bridge prototypes with identical spans.
Vary only one structural element, such as adding triangular braces.
Record the load each bridge carries before failure.
Build a voxel replica and explain the strongest shape.
hints: Triangles help structures resist deforming. Can you compare a rectangle and a triangle?
brothers: One builds while the other records measurements; switch for the second design.
stretch: Create a graph of load capacity versus bridge mass.

title: Starship Navigator
description: Chart the night sky and create a fictional navigation system from real astronomy.
steps: Use Stellarium to identify five real constellations or bright stars.
Record their seasonal visibility and approximate direction.
Draw a star map for a science-fiction explorer.
Explain how the map differs from real GPS and celestial navigation.
hints: Choose one bright star and find its name and direction before adding others.
brothers: One researches stars and the other illustrates the chart.
stretch: Model the phases of the Moon accurately across a month.

title: Music Reactor
description: Code an original electronic soundtrack for your own video game.
steps: Make a short beat with Sonic Pi.
Create an original melody using a small set of notes.
Change tempo and instruments to fit different scenes.
Export or record your own music and share a version with your brother.
hints: Start with a simple four-beat loop, then change one sound every four measures.
brothers: One creates percussion and the other invents a melody; combine both.
stretch: Write code that changes the music when the imaginary spaceship enters danger.

title: City of Tomorrow
description: Design a beautiful city with transit, clean water, energy, parks, and places to live.
steps: Decide on five services a good city must provide.
Sketch districts and major transportation routes.
Build the city together in a private Luanti world.
Test a disaster scenario and redesign a weak part.
hints: Start with roads, water, power, homes, and a school. Then let the skyline grow.
brothers: Each brother builds one district; connect both with a transport network.
stretch: Measure walking distances and redesign streets for efficiency.

title: The AI Detective Agency
description: Learn to catch convincing-sounding AI mistakes by investigating facts and sources.
steps: Write three science questions with verifiable answers.
Ask a supervised AI or use pre-written answer cards.
Check every factual claim against two reputable references.
Create a detective poster explaining how you checked the answers.
hints: Try a claim that sounds believable but has a measurable quantity.
brothers: One proposes claims; the other checks them, then reverse roles.
stretch: Design a checklist to catch misleading citations or invented experiments.

title: Solar Dome Survival
description: Build a mini greenhouse and investigate light, heat, power, and plant growth.
steps: Design two small identical plant environments.
Change one variable, such as light duration or temperature.
Measure and graph observations over several days.
Apply your findings to a solar dome in your game world.
hints: Choose a single variable and record observations before you change the design.
brothers: One gathers daily measurements; the other updates the chart, then swap.
stretch: Estimate how much solar-panel area a small greenhouse would need.

title: Inventor’s Identity Studio
description: Create a spectacular logo and poster for a fictional invention company.
steps: Pick three words describing your invention brand.
Sketch two symbols with different shapes.
Build a scalable vector logo and a poster with purposeful typography.
Get feedback and improve readability at small sizes.
hints: The best logo often works in plain black and white first.
brothers: One acts as designer and the other as demanding—but kind—client.
stretch: Create a complete identity kit: logo, colors, typography, and icon family.

title: Build Your Own Arcade
description: Code an original 2D game and design its characters, rules, difficulty, and soundtrack.
steps: Write a one-paragraph game idea and three simple rules.
Prototype the main interaction in Scratch or Godot.
Make or draw all your own art, sound, and levels.
Playtest with your brother and iterate based on evidence.
hints: Make a playable character with one action before drawing every background.
brothers: One programs interactions while the other makes visuals and sounds. Switch later.
stretch: Add an accessible tutorial and two distinct levels with measured difficulty.

title: Weather Station Alpha
description: Build a local data station that measures temperature or light over time.
steps: Choose a compatible sensor and read its data sheet.
With an adult, connect it to a Pico 2 W using 3.3V logic.
Write code to log measurements with timestamps.
Graph the results and explain unusual readings.
hints: Make a measurement every ten seconds. Observe whether the data changes as expected.
brothers: One handles hardware checks; the other creates the graph and report.
stretch: Add an alert threshold and document false positives.

title: Underwater Odyssey
description: Build a marine research city and investigate buoyancy, pressure, and ecology.
steps: Research the effects of increasing water pressure with depth.
Sketch a research habitat and emergency escape route.
Construct a submerged station in a Luanti world.
Make a museum room with accurate facts about three ocean species.
hints: Real pressure increases with depth. How would that affect windows and hulls?
brothers: One designs marine habitats while the other creates the lab and transport routes.
stretch: Explain pressure using an equation and depth comparison.

title: Invention for Someone Else
description: Use your skills to make something that makes real life easier for someone you care about.
steps: Ask a family member what small inconvenience they actually have.
List constraints, including cost, safety, and usability.
Build a cardboard, code, or electronics prototype.
Watch them use it, gather feedback, and revise.
hints: The most useful inventions solve an actual need, not just something exciting to build.
brothers: Interview separately, then combine ideas and build together.
stretch: Make accessible instructions so another family can reproduce the solution.

title: Interplanetary Radio
description: Invent a reliable way for an imaginary rover to send information back to Earth.
steps: Learn how signal travel time depends on distance and light speed.
Create a short binary message and an error-checking scheme.
Build a simple sender-receiver simulation in Python.
Explain why real-time joystick driving is difficult on Mars.
hints: Think about the time it takes a signal to cross millions of kilometers.
brothers: One programs a sender; the other designs and decodes the receiver.
stretch: Simulate corrupted bits and try a parity check.

title: The Clockwork Creature
description: Design a moving creature using mechanical joints and animation principles.
steps: Draw a creature and identify its joints.
Build a low-poly model or block sculpture in Blockbench.
Animate a simple repeating walking cycle.
Explain how a real motor might drive one joint.
hints: Model a single leg before making an entire creature.
brothers: One creates anatomy and appearance; the other plans the motion.
stretch: Make the walking loop believable at two speeds.

title: The Library of Wonders
description: Turn offline reference material into an extraordinary, source-grounded museum.
steps: Choose a scientific topic worth teaching.
Collect reliable offline references and record their sources.
Create a museum or booklet with three claims and supporting evidence.
Give your brother a tour and invite a challenge question.
hints: Pick one question and find a source that contains a measurable answer.
brothers: One researches and cites; the other designs the exhibition.
stretch: Build a retrieval index and check that every statement traces to a source.

title: The Crystal Cartographer
description: Explore the hidden world of rocks and minerals, then make an evidence-based geology atlas.
steps: Collect three safe rock samples, photograph them, and label where each was found without damaging protected sites.
Observe color, texture, grain size and any visible layers with a magnifying glass.
Compare observations with a trusted geology reference; distinguish what you know from what you are guessing.
Make a digital exhibit: an illustrated map, labeled photos, and one unanswered question.
hints: Start with three visible properties: color, texture and grain size. Which observations can another person repeat?
brothers: One is the field observer and the other checks reference sources; then swap.
stretch: Use a safe hardness comparison and discuss why appearances alone may misidentify minerals.

title: Echo Isles Soundscape
description: Give a world its own sound: record, layer and edit original audio to tell a story.
steps: Choose a scene and write five emotions or sensations you want the sound to evoke.
Record three original sounds using a microphone with adult-approved privacy precautions.
Use Audacity to trim, layer and adjust volume levels; avoid clipping.
Play your composition for your brother. Ask what place or mood he imagined and revise one element.
hints: A soundscape only needs three ingredients: an atmosphere, a rhythm, and one surprising detail.
brothers: One records ambient sound and one edits; swap halfway through.
stretch: Make two versions—calm and mysterious—using the same source recordings.
